title: Business Plan
summary: A traditional business plan that describes a company, its market, its products or services, how it will sell them, who runs it and how it will be financed, ending in financial projections. It follows the U.S. Small Business Administration's traditional plan structure and is written for lenders, investors, partners and the owners themselves.
audience: Lenders, investors and prospective partners deciding whether to fund or join the business, plus the owners using the plan to run it.
tone: Confident, concrete and businesslike: specific numbers and named markets, realistic rather than promotional, with no hype or unsupported superlatives.
preamble: You are an experienced small-business advisor helping the owner write a traditional business plan of the kind lenders and investors expect. Write in the company's voice ("we" or the company name), in plain business English. Prefer specific figures, named customer segments, named competitors and dated milestones over general claims; where a figure is not available in the sources or notes, leave a clearly marked placeholder such as [projected year-one revenue] rather than inventing one. Keep every number consistent across sections: the funding request, use of funds, sales forecast and financial projections must agree with each other. State assumptions behind forecasts explicitly. Do not make promises of returns, and do not describe the business as risk-free.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.guidance: Give the reader the whole plan in brief: what the company is, what it sells, to whom, and why it will succeed. Include the mission statement, the leadership and team size, the location, and a short statement of financial standing. If the plan seeks financing, say how much and what it is for, and summarise the growth plans. Write it last so it matches the rest of the plan, and keep it short enough that a lender can decide from it whether to read on.
elements: Mission statement
Products or services and the customers they serve
Leadership, number of employees and location
Current financial standing or key traction figures
Funding sought and its purpose (if seeking financing)
Growth plans or goals for the next one to three years

sections.heading: Company Description
sections.guidance: Describe the company in detail: the specific problem it solves and the consumers, organisations or businesses it serves. Explain the competitive advantages that will make it succeed, such as experienced staff, a distinctive location or a proprietary method, and why a competitor could not easily copy them. Give the company's history, current stage and location. Be specific about the customer need rather than describing the company in general terms. Leave legal structure, ownership and people to Organization and Management.
elements: Problem the business solves, stated in customer terms
Customers, organisations or businesses served
Competitive advantages (people, location, expertise, technology) and why they are hard to copy
Company history and current stage
Location and service area
sourcesNeeded: founder notes or company fact sheet

sections.heading: Market Analysis
sections.guidance: Show that you understand your industry and target market, using research rather than assertion. Describe industry outlook and trends, define the target market and its size, and analyse the main competitors: what they do well, where they fall short and how you will differentiate. Explain what successful businesses in this space do and how you will do it better. Cite the source and date of every market figure.
elements: Industry description, size and outlook
Target market defined with demographics or firmographics
Market size estimate with source and method
Named competitors with strengths and weaknesses
Differentiation from competitors
Relevant trends, regulations or barriers to entry

sections.heading: Organization and Management
sections.guidance: Explain how the business is structured and who runs it. State the legal structure (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation or LLC) and, for a corporation, whether it is a C or S corporation. Present an organisational chart or a clear description of roles and reporting lines, and give each key person's relevant experience and how it contributes to the company's success. Include ownership stakes, the board or advisors, and roles still to be hired.
elements: Legal structure
Organisational chart or description of roles and reporting lines
Key people with relevant experience and responsibilities
Ownership breakdown
Board members or advisors (if any)
Planned hires and staffing gaps
sourcesNeeded: resumes or bios of owners and key staff

sections.heading: Service or Product Line
sections.guidance: Describe what you sell or the service you offer, and how it benefits customers. Explain the product lifecycle, from development stage to launch and planned improvements. Note any intellectual property such as patents, copyrights or trademarks, filed or planned, and any research and development under way. Describe benefits in customer terms, not only features. Leave pricing strategy to Marketing and Sales, but give the cost and margin of each offering here.
elements: Description of each product or service
Customer benefit for each offering
Cost to produce or deliver, and margin
Product lifecycle or development stage
Intellectual property (patents, trademarks, copyrights) filed or planned
Research and development plans

sections.heading: Marketing and Sales
sections.guidance: Explain how you will attract and keep customers and how a sale actually happens. Choose the strategy that fits this business and follows from the market analysis: describe positioning, pricing, promotion and the channels you will use, and the sales process from first contact to closed sale. Give costs for the main marketing activities. Tie the sales forecast to these activities and state its assumptions (for example leads per month, conversion rate, average order value).
elements: Positioning and value proposition for the target market
Pricing strategy
Marketing and promotion channels
Sales process from lead to closed sale
Customer retention approach
Sales forecast with stated assumptions

sections.heading: Funding Request
sections.guidance: Include this section when the plan asks for financing. State how much funding you need over the next five years and exactly what it will be used for (equipment, salaries, specific bills, working capital). Say whether you want debt or equity, the terms you would like, and the period the request covers. Describe any longer-term financial plans, such as paying off debt or selling the business. The amounts must match the financial projections.
elements: Amount requested
Debt or equity, with preferred terms
Detailed use of funds
Time period the request covers
Future funding needs over the next five years
Long-term financial plans (repayment, buyout, sale)
sourcesNeeded: quotes for equipment or major purchases

sections.heading: Financial Projections
sections.guidance: Convince the reader that the business is stable and will be a financial success. For an established business, include historical income statements, balance sheets and cash flow statements, usually for the last three to five years, and any collateral you could pledge. Provide a prospective financial outlook for the next five years, with forecast income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements and capital expenditure budgets; break the first year into quarterly or monthly figures. State the assumptions behind every forecast and explain how the figures connect to the funding request. Include a break-even analysis showing the sales volume at which the business covers its costs.
elements: Historical income statements, balance sheets and cash flow statements (established businesses)
Projected income statements for five years
Projected balance sheets and cash flow statements
First-year figures broken out monthly or quarterly
Capital expenditure budget
Key assumptions behind the forecasts
Break-even analysis
Collateral available (if seeking a loan)
dataNeeded: projected revenue and expenses by period

sections.heading: Appendix
sections.guidance: Collect supporting documents the reader may ask for: credit histories, resumes, product pictures, letters of reference, licences, permits, patents, legal documents and other contracts. List each item with a one-line description so the reader knows what it supports. Do not put arguments here that belong in the main sections.
elements: List of supporting documents with one-line descriptions
Resumes of key people
Permits, licences and legal documents
Letters of reference or intent

rubric.criterion: Market evidence: the target market, its size and the competition are defined with cited research rather than assertion.

levels.descriptor: Target customers are precisely defined. Market size is estimated with a stated method and dated sources. Named competitors are analysed honestly, and differentiation follows from that analysis.
Market and competitors are described with some sourced figures, but sizing method or competitor analysis is thin in places.
Market is described in broad terms ("everyone who…") with few sources. Competitors are listed without real analysis or dismissed.
No credible market definition or sizing. Claims such as "no competition" or unsourced large market figures carry the argument.

rubric.criterion: Financial credibility: projections are complete, grounded in stated assumptions and realistic for the business and market.

levels.descriptor: Five-year projected income, balance sheet and cash flow are present, with first-year detail. Every forecast rests on explicit, defensible assumptions tied to the market and sales sections. Historical figures are included where the business has a history.
Core statements are present and mostly reasoned, but some assumptions are unstated or optimistic, or first-year detail is missing.
Projections are partial (for example, revenue only) or assumptions are mostly missing. Growth rates look arbitrary.
Financials are absent, unsupported or implausible, and a lender could not judge the business's ability to repay or return capital.

rubric.criterion: Internal consistency: figures, names and claims agree across every section of the plan.

levels.descriptor: Funding amount, use of funds, sales forecast, headcount and projections match everywhere they appear. The executive summary reflects the body exactly.
One or two minor mismatches (a rounded figure, a renamed product) that do not change the picture.
Several contradictions, such as a funding request that does not match the projections or a summary that promises what the body does not support.
Sections contradict each other on core numbers or strategy, so the reader cannot tell which version is true.

rubric.criterion: Funding case: the request states how much is needed, on what terms, for what, and how the money returns.

levels.descriptor: Amount, debt or equity, preferred terms, period covered and an itemised use of funds are all stated, and repayment or return follows plausibly from the projections.
Amount and use of funds are clear, but terms, period or the path to repayment are vague.
An amount is named but use of funds is a lump sum or the terms are missing.
The request is unclear or unjustified: no amount, no use of funds, or no link to the business's finances.

provenance.source: U.S. Small Business Administration, "Write your business plan" (traditional business plan format, nine sections including the appendix)

title: Design Doc / RFC
summary: A technical design document or request for comments (RFC) that proposes how to build or change a software system, before the work starts. It states the problem and goals, describes the proposed design in enough detail for peers to review, compares the alternatives, and covers security, rollout, testing and open risks so reviewers can approve, push back or decide.
audience: Engineers, tech leads and architects who will review, approve or build the proposed system, plus adjacent teams (security, SRE, product) who need to understand its impact.
tone: Precise, direct and neutral: engineer to engineer, making the reasoning and trade-offs explicit rather than selling the proposal.
preamble: You are a senior software engineer writing a design document (RFC) for peer review. The purpose is to get a decision: make the proposal concrete enough that a reviewer can find its flaws, and state the trade-offs honestly rather than advocating. Name actual components, interfaces, data and numbers rather than describing them in general terms. Separate what is decided, what is proposed and what is still open, and label assumptions as assumptions. Never invent benchmarks, capacity figures, incident history, dates or owners; where a figure the design depends on is not in the material, leave a clearly marked placeholder such as [TBD: p99 latency target]. Prefer short paragraphs, bulleted lists and tables for comparisons; describe diagrams in words or as simple Mermaid or ASCII sketches only when the material supports them. Use consistent names for every component throughout the document.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.guidance: Write a short summary a busy reviewer can read alone: the problem in one or two sentences, what you propose to do, and the decision or feedback you need from reviewers. Mention the expected impact (who or what changes) and any deadline that drives the decision. Open with a status block, one field per line with bold labels: **Status:** (Draft unless the material says otherwise), **Authors:**, **Reviewers:** and **Last updated:**. Fill each field from the material and leave an unknown field blank after its label rather than guessing. Draft or revise this summary after the design sections so it matches what the document actually proposes.
elements: The problem in one or two sentences
The proposed solution in one or two sentences
The decision or feedback requested from reviewers
Expected impact or affected systems and teams
Status block: authors, reviewers, status and last-updated date

sections.heading: Context and Motivation
sections.guidance: Explain the current state of the system and why it is no longer good enough. Give the reader the background a capable engineer outside the team would need: the relevant components, how they behave today, and the evidence of the problem (incidents, metrics, user reports, upcoming requirements). Say why now: what happens if nothing changes. Keep design ideas out of this section.
elements: Description of the current system or process
The specific problem or limitation
Evidence of the problem (metrics, incidents, user or customer reports)
Why this needs addressing now, and the cost of doing nothing
Links to prior designs, tickets or discussions
dataNeeded: Current performance, reliability or cost metrics

sections.heading: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.guidance: List the goals as specific, testable outcomes, with target numbers where they exist (for example a latency, error-rate or cost target). Then list non-goals: reasonable things a reader might expect this work to do that it deliberately will not, with a brief reason. Note hard constraints (deadlines, compatibility, budget, compliance) separately. Every goal should be something the design and testing sections can be checked against.
elements: Goals stated as measurable or verifiable outcomes
Explicit non-goals, each with a brief reason
Hard constraints (deadline, compatibility, budget, compliance)
A target number or pass condition for each goal that has one

sections.heading: Proposed Design
sections.guidance: Describe the design in enough detail that a reviewer can judge whether it works and an engineer could start building it. Start with a high-level overview of the components and how they interact, then go into the parts that matter: interfaces and APIs, data model and storage, key flows (request path, write path, failure path), and how the design meets each goal. Call out the key design decisions and the reasoning behind each, and state assumptions explicitly. Use sub-headings, tables or a simple diagram description when they make the structure easier to follow.
sections.lengthHint: The longest section; as long as the design needs
elements: High-level overview of components and their interactions
Interfaces or API contracts (endpoints, signatures, schemas)
Data model and storage changes
Key flows, including error and failure handling
Key design decisions with their rationale
How the design meets each stated goal

sections.heading: Alternatives Considered
sections.guidance: Describe the serious alternatives you considered, including doing nothing and buying or reusing an existing solution where that is plausible. For each, summarise how it would work, its advantages and its drawbacks against the goals, and why it was rejected. Treat the alternatives fairly; a reviewer should be able to disagree with your choice using only this section. A comparison table works well when there are three or more options.
sections.lengthHint: A paragraph or table row per alternative
elements: At least two alternatives, including doing nothing where relevant
Pros and cons of each against the stated goals
The reason each alternative was rejected
A comparison of trade-offs (table or summary)
sourcesNeeded: Comparable systems at other teams or companies
dataNeeded: Cost, effort or performance estimates per option

sections.heading: Cross-cutting Concerns
sections.guidance: Cover how the design affects security, privacy, performance and scalability, reliability, observability and cost. For each concern, say what changes, what the risk is and how the design addresses it; write 'No change' with a one-line reason rather than omitting a concern. Name the data handled and who can access it, the expected load and limits, how failures are detected (metrics, logs, alerts, dashboards) and the expected operating cost. Use one short sub-section or bullet group per concern.
sections.lengthHint: A short paragraph or bullet group per concern
elements: Security: authentication, authorisation, threat model or attack surface changes
Privacy: personal or sensitive data handled, retention and access
Performance and scalability: expected load, limits and bottlenecks
Reliability: failure modes, redundancy and recovery
Observability: metrics, logs, alerts and dashboards
Cost: infrastructure or licensing impact
sourcesNeeded: Threat model or security review checklist

sections.heading: Rollout and Migration
sections.guidance: Explain how the change reaches production safely. Describe the phases (for example behind a feature flag, internal users, a percentage rollout, general availability), how existing data, clients or APIs migrate, and how backwards compatibility is kept during the transition. State the rollback plan and the signals that would trigger it. Note dependencies on other teams and any communication users or operators need.
elements: Rollout phases with entry and exit criteria
Data or client migration steps
Backwards compatibility during the transition
Rollback plan and the signals that trigger it
Dependencies on other teams and a rough timeline

sections.heading: Testing Plan
sections.guidance: Describe how you will know the design works and keeps working. Cover the levels of testing that apply (unit, integration, end-to-end, load or performance, security, migration dry runs) and what each one verifies. Tie tests back to the goals and to the riskiest parts of the design, and say how success is measured after launch. Mention test environments or data the plan needs.
elements: Test levels and what each verifies
Tests mapped to the stated goals and riskiest components
Performance or load testing approach where relevant
Post-launch validation metrics or acceptance criteria
Test environments or data required
sourcesNeeded: Existing test strategy or coverage reports

sections.heading: Risks and Open Questions
sections.guidance: List the main risks to the design or the project, each with its likelihood or impact and a mitigation. Then list the open questions that reviewers can help answer, phrased as specific questions with an owner or a decision date where known. Do not hide uncertainty elsewhere in the document; gather it here so reviewers can focus on it.
sections.lengthHint: Two bulleted lists or a risk table
elements: Key risks, each with impact or likelihood
A mitigation for each risk
Open questions phrased as specific questions
Owner or decision date for each open question where known

sections.heading: Decision Log
sections.guidance: Record decisions made during review as a table with the columns Date, Decision, Decided by and Rationale, newest last, so later readers understand why the design looks the way it does. Each entry gives the date, the decision, who made or approved it, and a one-line rationale or link to the discussion. Include decisions to reject or defer, and update the relevant sections when a decision changes the design.
elements: Dated entries for each decision
The decision and who made or approved it
A one-line rationale or link to the discussion

rubric.criterion: Design specificity: the proposed design is concrete enough to review and build from.

levels.descriptor: Components, interfaces, data model and key flows (including failure paths) are named and described precisely; a reviewer could find flaws and an engineer could start building without guessing.
The main components and flows are clear, but some interfaces, data changes or failure handling are left vague.
Describes the design at a high level only; important mechanics are hand-waved or missing, so reviewers cannot judge whether it works.
Reads as an aspiration or a list of technologies rather than a design; there is nothing concrete to review.

rubric.criterion: Goal traceability: goals are measurable and the design, rollout and tests demonstrably serve them.

levels.descriptor: Goals are specific and measurable, non-goals set clear boundaries, and every goal is visibly addressed by the design and verified in the testing plan.
Goals are mostly measurable and addressed, but one or two lack a target, a clear link to the design, or a test.
Goals are vague or non-goals are missing; the connection between goals, design and tests is loose.
Goals are absent or unrelated to the design; there is no way to tell whether the design succeeds.

rubric.criterion: Trade-off analysis: alternatives are treated fairly and the choice is justified.

levels.descriptor: Considers the realistic alternatives (including doing nothing where relevant), compares them on the stated goals fairly, and gives a clear, convincing reason for the choice and its costs.
Covers the main alternatives with reasonable pros and cons, but the comparison is uneven or a cost of the chosen design is understated.
Alternatives are straw men or listed without real comparison; the rationale for the chosen design is thin.
No alternatives are considered, or the choice is asserted without justification.

rubric.criterion: Risk and operability: risks, failure modes, rollout and rollback are planned, and uncertainty is stated openly.

levels.descriptor: Security, privacy, reliability and observability are each addressed; rollout is phased with a concrete rollback trigger; risks have mitigations and open questions are specific and owned.
Most concerns and risks are covered, but a concern is skipped, the rollback plan is generic, or open questions lack owners.
Operational concerns and risks are mentioned only briefly; no clear rollback plan; uncertainty is hidden in the prose.
Ignores security, failure modes and rollout; presents the design as risk-free.

provenance.source: Hand-written from common engineering design-doc and RFC practice; the anthropics/skills doc-coauthoring skill was consulted as inspiration only

title: How-to guide (Diátaxis)
summary: A goal-oriented guide that walks an already-competent reader through the steps needed to get a specific real-world task done, such as configuring, deploying or troubleshooting something. It contains actions, not lessons: explanation and full reference detail are linked rather than included. Follows the how-to guide form of the Diátaxis documentation framework.
audience: Practitioners who already know the product and its basic concepts and need to accomplish one specific task now, usually in the middle of their own work.
tone: Direct, practical and economical: imperative and conditional imperative mood, second person, no marketing, no digressions.
preamble: You are an experienced technical writer producing a how-to guide in the Diátaxis sense: directions that take a competent user to a goal they have already chosen. Write only what the reader must do and the minimum they must know to do it. Do not teach concepts, justify design choices, or survey alternatives; when background or full option lists matter, point to the relevant reference or explanation instead of including it. Frame the guide around the user's goal and the problem they face, not around the tool's features or menus. The guide need not cover a whole workflow end to end: start where the reader's task starts and stop when the goal is reached, preferring what is practically useful over completeness. Use imperatives and conditional imperatives ("To keep existing data, run…", "If the service fails to start, check…"), keep steps in the order the reader will perform them, and allow for forks where real situations differ. Assume basic competence; do not explain how to open a terminal or what a file is unless the type's audience demands it. Use code blocks for commands, file contents and expected output, and mark values the reader must replace with clear placeholders such as <PROJECT_ID>. Never invent commands, flags, file paths, settings, version numbers or URLs: take them from the sources or the writer's notes, and where one is unknown write a visible placeholder like "[command needed]".

sections.heading: Goal
sections.guidance: State in one or two sentences what the reader will have accomplished when they finish, phrased as a practical outcome ("This guide shows how to rotate the API signing key without downtime"). Name the situation it applies to so readers can tell quickly whether they are in the right place. Do not explain why the feature exists or how it works internally; at most link to an explanation. The document title should read "How to <task>".
elements: Title phrased as "How to <task>"
Outcome stated as a concrete task the reader will complete
Situation or context in which the guide applies
No conceptual explanation beyond one clause (links instead)
sourcesNeeded: Product documentation or ticket describing the task
User question or support request the guide answers

sections.heading: Before You Begin
sections.guidance: List what must already be true before the first step: access and permissions, installed tools with minimum versions, accounts, and any earlier task the reader should have completed. Keep it a short bulleted list of conditions, not instructions for meeting them; link to the guide or reference that covers each one. Skip anything a competent member of the audience can be assumed to have.
elements: Required access, roles or permissions
Tools or software with minimum versions
Prior tasks or configuration, linked rather than explained
Assumed competence stated briefly where it is not obvious

sections.heading: Steps
sections.guidance: Write a numbered sequence of actions in the order the reader performs them, one action per step, each starting with an imperative verb. Use conditional imperatives where the path depends on the reader's situation ("If you use a managed database, skip to step 5"), and split the guide into short sub-headed parts (###) when the task has distinct phases. Put commands, configuration and expected output in code blocks, with placeholders for values the reader supplies. Include only the explanation needed to choose between branches or avoid a destructive mistake, and give warnings before the step they apply to, not after.
elements: Numbered, ordered actions each starting with an imperative verb
Exact commands, settings or UI paths in code blocks or bold
Placeholders marked for values the reader must supply
Conditional branches for situations that genuinely differ
Warnings placed before risky or irreversible steps
No teaching, history or feature tours between steps
sourcesNeeded: CLI or API reference for the commands used
Release notes for the version covered
Engineer's working notes or a tested runbook

sections.heading: Verify the Result
sections.guidance: Tell the reader how to confirm the task worked: a command to run, a page to check, or a log line to look for, together with what success looks like. If there are common failure signs, list each with the single most likely fix or a link to the troubleshooting reference. Keep it to checks and fixes, not a discussion of causes.
elements: A concrete check the reader can perform
What a successful result looks like (expected output or state)
Common failure signs with a fix or link

sections.heading: Related Reference
sections.guidance: Give a short list of links to the material the guide deliberately left out: full reference for the commands and settings used, the explanation of the underlying concepts, and related how-to guides for neighbouring tasks. Label each link with what the reader will find there. Do not summarise the linked content. Use only links that appear in the sources or the writer's notes; where a needed page is known to exist but its URL is not given, write the page name with a visible "[link needed]" placeholder. Omit the section if there is genuinely nothing to point to.
elements: Reference for the main commands, APIs or settings used in the steps
Link to an explanation of the underlying concept
Related how-to guides for next or adjacent tasks
Each link labelled with what the reader will find

rubric.criterion: Goal orientation: the guide is framed around a real task the user wants to accomplish, not around the tool's features.

levels.descriptor: The title and goal name a concrete user task and situation; every step moves the reader toward that outcome and nothing exists only to show off a feature.
The goal is clear and task-shaped, but a step or two drifts into describing features or options the reader does not need for this task.
The guide is organised around the product (a menu, a command, a feature) more than a user goal; the reader has to work out which parts serve their task.
No identifiable user goal; the document is a feature tour or reference dump presented as a guide.

rubric.criterion: Actionability: a competent reader can follow the steps in order and finish the task without guessing.

levels.descriptor: Every step is one imperative action with exact commands, values or UI paths; placeholders are clearly marked; the order matches what the reader actually does; nothing required is missing.
Steps are followable, but one or two combine several actions, leave a value implicit, or omit a minor step an experienced reader can infer.
Several steps are vague ("configure the service appropriately"), out of order, or missing commands; the reader must consult other material to proceed.
The task cannot be completed from the guide: key steps are missing, wrong, or described only in general terms.

rubric.criterion: Action, not explanation: teaching, background and full reference detail are left out and linked instead.

levels.descriptor: The guide contains only actions and the minimum context needed to choose a branch or avoid harm; concepts and exhaustive options are linked from Related Reference.
Mostly action, with an occasional paragraph of background or a list of options that could have been a link.
Explanation and reference material are interleaved with the steps often enough to slow the reader and hide the actions.
Reads as a tutorial or explanation; the actual steps are buried in teaching or digressions.

rubric.criterion: Real-world adaptability: the guide handles the situations real users meet, including forks, risks and confirming success.

levels.descriptor: Genuine variations are handled with conditional imperatives; warnings precede risky steps; prerequisites are stated; the reader can verify success and recognise common failures.
Handles the main path well and most variations, but one realistic fork, warning or success check is missing.
Assumes a single ideal environment; important variations, prerequisites or warnings are absent, so many readers will get stuck.
Ignores real conditions entirely; following it in a typical environment is likely to fail or cause damage without warning.

provenance.source: Diátaxis documentation framework, "How-to guides" (Daniele Procida, diataxis.fr): principles paraphrased; the section list is own text following common technical-writing practice, not prescribed by Diátaxis

title: Tutorial (Diátaxis)
summary: A learning-oriented lesson in which a beginner, guided step by step, builds or does something concrete and gains skill and confidence through the doing rather than through explanation. Every step produces a visible result, the route is fixed and known to work, and explanation is kept to a minimum with links for later. Follows the tutorial form of the Diátaxis documentation framework.
audience: Newcomers to the product or technology who want to learn it by doing, with little prior knowledge and no particular task of their own to finish yet.
tone: Encouraging, concrete and patient: first-person plural ("we"), short sentences, present tense, frequent confirmation that things are going right, no jargon left undefined.
preamble: You are an experienced technical writer and teacher producing a tutorial in the Diátaxis sense: a guided lesson in which the reader learns by doing something meaningful under your direction. You are responsible for the learner's success, so the path must be one fixed route that works every time for a beginner on a typical setup. Write as the teacher alongside the learner, using "we" ("Now we add a route…"), and keep the reader acting: every step is a concrete action followed by a visible result they can check. Keep explanation to the minimum needed to carry on, one short clause at most, and link to explanation material for the rest; do not offer options, alternatives, best-practice digressions or abstract concepts, even when they would be more correct in general. Get the learner to a first visible result within the first few steps and keep results coming. Show the expected output after actions that produce it, point out what the learner should notice in it, and warn about the mistakes beginners commonly make at the point where they would make them. State at the start what the learner will build or achieve, without promising what they will understand. Use code blocks for commands, file contents and output, and give complete file contents or exact edits rather than fragments the learner must assemble. Never invent commands, flags, file paths, package names, output or version numbers: take them from the sources or the writer's notes, and where one is unknown write a visible placeholder like "[command needed]" or "[expected output needed]".

sections.heading: What You Will Build
sections.guidance: Tell the learner in a few sentences what they will have made or done by the end, as a concrete, visible result ("By the end we will have a small web app that lists books from a local database"). A screenshot description or sample of the final output helps them picture the destination. Describe what they will do, not what they will learn or understand; avoid promises such as "you will master". Give a realistic time estimate if the sources support one.
elements: Concrete end result the learner will have built or done
Picture of the destination (sample output, screenshot or description)
Framed as what we will do, not as learning outcomes
Approximate time to complete, if known
sourcesNeeded: Finished example project or working demo
dataNeeded: Final output or screenshot of the finished result

sections.heading: Before You Start
sections.guidance: Get the learner to a known, working starting point. Name the operating systems or environments the tutorial was tested on, then walk through any installation or setup as explicit steps with a check that it worked (for example a version command and its output). Keep assumed knowledge to the minimum a beginner has, and say plainly what it is. Do not list alternative installers or configurations; pick one route.
elements: Environment and versions the tutorial was tested on
Exact installation or setup steps along one route
A check that setup worked, with expected output
Assumed prior knowledge stated briefly

sections.heading: Steps
sections.guidance: Lead the learner through a single linear path in small numbered steps, grouped under short ### sub-headings when the work has distinct stages. Each step asks for one action and then shows the result the learner should see, so they can confirm they are on track before moving on; the first visible result should come within the first two or three steps. After showing output, point out the one thing the learner should notice in it ("Notice that the new book now appears at the top of the list"). Give complete code or exact edits, show expected output in code blocks, and add a brief warning where beginners commonly go wrong ("If you see 'port already in use', stop the earlier server first"). Explain only enough to keep going, in a clause, and link out for depth; never branch into options or alternatives.
elements: One linear path with no options or alternatives
Each step a single concrete action phrased with "we"
First visible result within the first two or three steps
Visible, checkable result after each meaningful step
Expected output shown in code blocks, with what to notice in it
Warnings at the points where beginners commonly go wrong
Explanation limited to a clause per step, with links for more
sourcesNeeded: Tested working example or sample repository
CLI or API reference for the commands used
Support questions or common beginner errors
dataNeeded: Common error messages and their fixes

sections.heading: What You Built
sections.guidance: Recap what the learner has now made and the things they did along the way, so they recognise their own progress. Point to the finished result they can see or run. Keep it brief and concrete, and do not introduce new concepts or steps here.
elements: Summary of the finished result the learner now has
The main things the learner did, in order
No new concepts or instructions introduced

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.guidance: Give the learner a short list of where to go next: a follow-on tutorial, how-to guides for tasks they are likely to attempt now, and explanation pages for the concepts the tutorial deliberately skipped. Label each link with what the reader will get from it. Do not summarise the linked material.
elements: Follow-on tutorial, if one exists
How-to guides for likely next tasks
Explanation pages for concepts skipped in the tutorial
Each link labelled with what the reader will find

rubric.criterion: Learning by doing: the learner is kept acting, and each step ends in a visible result they can check.

levels.descriptor: Every step is a concrete action followed by a result the learner can see and compare against shown output; the first result arrives within the first few steps; there are no stretches of reading without doing.
Nearly every step produces a checkable result, but one or two omit the expected output or bundle several actions together.
Many steps lack visible results or expected output, so the learner often cannot tell whether they are on track.
Mostly description or explanation; the learner does little and has no way to confirm progress.

rubric.criterion: Reliability: a beginner following the tutorial exactly on the stated setup reaches the promised result.

levels.descriptor: Setup is explicit and checked; every command, code listing and output is complete and consistent; common beginner mistakes are anticipated where they occur.
The path works, but a minor gap (an unstated version, a partial code fragment, a missing warning) could trip some learners.
Several gaps or inconsistencies between steps, code and output make failure likely for a beginner.
The tutorial cannot be completed as written: steps are missing, wrong, or depend on unstated setup.

rubric.criterion: Minimal explanation, single path: concepts, options and alternatives are left out and linked instead.

levels.descriptor: One fixed route throughout; explanation never exceeds a short clause per step and deeper material is linked; no alternatives or option lists appear.
Mostly a single focused path, with an occasional paragraph of background or a mentioned alternative that could have been cut or linked.
Frequent explanatory detours or choices for the learner interrupt the flow and dilute the lesson.
Reads as an explanation or reference with steps attached; the learner must make decisions they are not equipped to make.

rubric.criterion: Guided experience: the learner knows the destination at the start, feels accompanied along the way, and sees what they achieved at the end.

levels.descriptor: The destination is stated concretely up front without promising understanding; the voice is a supportive "we" throughout; the recap and next steps close the lesson and point onward.
Destination, voice and closing are present, but one is weak (a vague goal, inconsistent voice, or a thin recap).
The learner is not told where they are heading or what they built, or the voice is impersonal and instructional throughout.
No stated destination, recap or onward path; the learner is left without orientation.

title: Full and Individual Evaluation
summary: A school psychoeducational evaluation report, written for a multidisciplinary team, that brings together a student's background, the reason for referral, the assessments given, and the cognitive, academic and social-emotional results. It reviews the exclusionary factors and sets out the evidence the team will weigh when it decides special education eligibility, without stating that decision itself. Also called a psychoeducational evaluation or initial/re-evaluation report under IDEA.
audience: The multidisciplinary evaluation team and the student's parents or guardians (school psychologist or diagnostician, teachers, special education staff, administrators), who need an accurate, readable account of the evaluation to make an eligibility decision together.
tone: Professional, neutral and objective: plain language a parent can follow, person-first wording, strengths described alongside needs, and results reported without speculation or advocacy.
preamble: You are drafting a section of a Full and Individual Evaluation (FIE) report for a school multidisciplinary team, writing as the evaluation professional who conducted or compiled it. Write in professional, neutral prose that a parent without clinical training can follow; when you use a technical term (standard score, percentile, confidence interval, descriptive range), explain it briefly the first time. Use person-first language and refer to the student by first name or as "the student" consistently. Report only what the records, scores, observations and interviews in the material show; attribute each finding to its source (instrument, rater, observer or record) and date where known. Do not diagnose beyond what the material states, and do not state a final eligibility determination or disability classification: that is the team's decision. When you report several numeric scores, present them in a Markdown table (index or subtest, standard or scaled score, percentile, descriptive range, and confidence interval with its confidence level, such as 90% or 95%, where given) and interpret the pattern in prose around it, naming relative strengths and weaknesses. Never invent or round scores, and never convert between score types unless the material gives the conversion. If a score, date or instrument is missing, write a placeholder such as "[score needed]" rather than estimating. Keep student identifiers to those already in the material.

sections.heading: Student Background
sections.guidance: Summarize the background: identifying information, history, and relevant context present in the sources. Neutral, factual. Cover the student's age and grade, school and educational history (attendance, retentions, school changes, prior services or plans), relevant developmental, medical and health history including vision and hearing screening results and any motor or communication concerns, language background and the language(s) used at home and school, and family context only as it bears on learning. Note the student's strengths and interests as well as concerns. Attribute information to its source (parent interview, cumulative record, health record).
elements: Age, grade and current school placement
Educational history (attendance, school changes, retentions, prior services)
Developmental and health history, including vision and hearing screening and any motor or communication concerns
Home and dominant language background
Student strengths and interests
Source of each piece of background information
sourcesNeeded: Parent or guardian interview or developmental history form
dataNeeded: Date of birth and chronological age at testing
Vision and hearing screening results and dates

sections.heading: Reason for Referral
sections.guidance: State who requested the evaluation and why, the presenting concerns, prior interventions and their outcome, and the questions the evaluation will consider. Say whether this is an initial evaluation or a re-evaluation and give the referral and consent dates where the sources have them. Describe the general education interventions tried (type, frequency, duration, who delivered them) and the progress-monitoring results collected at regular intervals, including whether those results were shared with the parents. End with the specific referral questions, phrased as areas the evaluation will assess so later sections can address them with evidence (for example "What are the student's reading skills relative to grade-level expectations?"), not as yes/no questions about eligibility.
elements: Who referred the student and when
Initial evaluation or re-evaluation, with consent date
Presenting concerns in specific, observable terms
Prior interventions with frequency, duration, provider and outcome
Progress-monitoring results at regular intervals and whether they were shared with parents
Explicit referral questions, framed as areas to assess rather than yes/no eligibility questions

sections.heading: Assessment Procedures
sections.guidance: List the instruments and procedures used and the records reviewed, as found in the sources. For each instrument give its full name, the date given and the examiner's role; include observations, interviews and rating scales with the rater. Note which areas of suspected disability each procedure covers (for example cognitive, academic, communication, motor, social-emotional, adaptive). State the language and mode of administration and any accommodations or deviations from standard procedure. Close with a short statement on whether the results are considered a valid estimate of the student's current functioning, and why, based only on what the sources report about effort, rapport and conditions.
sections.lengthHint: A list or table plus a short validity paragraph
elements: Each standardized instrument with full name, date and examiner role
Observations, interviews and rating scales with setting and rater
Records reviewed
Areas of suspected disability each procedure addresses
Language and mode of administration, and any accommodations
Validity statement on effort, rapport and testing conditions
sourcesNeeded: Examiner testing notes and behavior observations
dataNeeded: List of evaluators and their roles

sections.heading: Cognitive Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe cognitive results grounded in the reported scores; interpret in plain language. Name the instrument, then present the composite and index scores in a table with percentiles, descriptive ranges and confidence intervals where given. Explain the overall pattern: relative strengths and weaknesses, and whether significant differences between indexes make an overall score less meaningful. Include relevant processing measures (for example phonological processing, memory, processing speed) and connect the findings to the referral questions and the classroom concerns.
elements: Instrument named with date of administration
Score table with composite and index scores, percentiles and descriptive ranges
Plain-language explanation of the score scale
Relative cognitive strengths and weaknesses
Note on index variability and how to interpret the overall score
Link from cognitive findings to the referral concerns
sourcesNeeded: Cognitive assessment score report (for example WISC-V, WJ IV COG, DAS-II, KABC-II)
dataNeeded: Index discrepancy or pairwise comparison results

sections.heading: Academic Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe academic achievement results (reading, writing, math) grounded in the reported scores. Present standardized achievement scores in a table by area and subtest, then interpret each area in prose: what the student can do, where skills break down, and how that matches classroom performance. Bring in curriculum-based measures, state or district assessment results, grades and work samples where the sources have them, so the standardized scores are seen alongside everyday performance. Cover oral language when it was assessed. When a specific learning disability is being considered, include the observation of the student's academic performance in the regular classroom (date, setting, observer, what was seen) and how the observed behavior relates to academic functioning.
sections.lengthHint: Score table plus a paragraph per academic area
elements: Achievement instrument named with date
Score table for reading, writing and math with percentiles and descriptive ranges
Interpretation of each academic area, including specific skill strengths and gaps
Classroom performance evidence (grades, curriculum-based measures, work samples)
State or district assessment results where available
Comparison of standardized results with classroom performance
Classroom observation of academic performance in the area of concern (required when a specific learning disability is considered)
sourcesNeeded: Achievement test score report (for example WIAT-4, WJ IV ACH, KTEA-3)

sections.heading: Social, Emotional & Behavioral
sections.guidance: Describe social, emotional and behavioral findings (rating scales, observations, interviews) present in the sources. For rating scales, name each rater (parent, teacher, student) and report elevated or at-risk scales in a table with T-scores and classification ranges, noting where raters agree or differ. Summarize direct observations with setting, date, duration and what was observed in behavioral terms. Include the student's own perspective from interview, and describe adaptive or social strengths as well as concerns.
elements: Rating scales named with each rater
Table of clinically significant and at-risk scales with T-scores
Agreement or disagreement across raters and settings
Direct observation with setting, date, duration and observed behavior
Student's own perspective from interview
Social and emotional strengths
sourcesNeeded: Behavior rating scale reports (for example BASC-3, Conners 4)
Student, parent and teacher interview notes
dataNeeded: Rating scale T-scores and classification ranges by rater

sections.heading: Consideration of Exclusionary Factors
sections.guidance: Describe the other factors the sources show were considered as possible explanations for the concerns, and what the sources say about each. Address each factor by name: lack of appropriate instruction in reading (including its essential components) and math, delivered by qualified staff; limited English proficiency; visual, hearing or motor impairment; cultural factors; environmental or economic disadvantage; and attendance, plus any others the sources raise. When a specific learning disability is being considered, also address whether intellectual disability or emotional disturbance could account for the concerns, citing the relevant findings. For each, cite the evidence reviewed (screenings, attendance, language data, instructional history). Report what the evidence shows; do not conclude whether a factor is or is not the primary cause, since that is the team's judgment.
sections.lengthHint: One short paragraph or table row per factor
elements: Appropriate instruction in reading and math by qualified staff, with evidence reviewed
Limited English proficiency, with language data
Vision, hearing and motor status, with screening results
Cultural, environmental and economic factors
Attendance and school changes
Intellectual disability and emotional disturbance, when a specific learning disability is considered
Evidence cited for each factor without a causal conclusion
sourcesNeeded: Home language survey and English proficiency assessment

sections.heading: Eligibility Determination
sections.guidance: Summarize the evidence the team will weigh. Present it as a draft basis for the team's discussion; do not state a conclusion. Organize the summary around the eligibility criteria the team is considering and the referral questions, pointing back to the relevant findings in earlier sections, including evidence that cuts both ways. Address both parts of the team's question as the sources inform them: whether the criteria for a disability condition appear to be met, and the evidence about educational need for specially designed instruction. For a specific learning disability, note which evidence bears on the pattern-of-strengths-and-weaknesses or response-to-intervention criteria the state uses, without applying them. Leave the determination itself to the team and say so in a closing sentence.
elements: Eligibility categories or criteria under consideration
Summary of findings mapped to each criterion
Evidence bearing on each referral question, citing the earlier section (no conclusion)
Evidence on educational need for specially designed instruction
Evidence that does not support eligibility, stated fairly
Explicit statement that the determination rests with the team
sourcesNeeded: Applicable state or district eligibility criteria
Findings from the earlier sections of this report
dataNeeded: Key scores and data points relevant to each criterion

sections.heading: Recommendations
sections.guidance: Recommended next steps and supports for the team to consider, grounded in the findings. Framed as recommendations, not decisions. Tie each recommendation to a specific finding, and group them by area (instruction, accommodations, behavior and social-emotional support, home, further evaluation). Make each one concrete enough to act on, and keep them appropriate regardless of the eligibility outcome, since the team has not yet decided.
elements: Each recommendation linked to a specific finding
Instructional strategies and interventions
Classroom and testing accommodations
Behavioral or social-emotional supports where indicated
Suggestions for home or family
Referrals or further evaluation where indicated
sourcesNeeded: Findings from the earlier sections of this report
Teacher and parent input on what has helped

rubric.criterion: Score reporting: scores are reported exactly as in the sources, with the right score type, percentile, descriptive range and confidence interval, tabulated and interpreted.

levels.descriptor: Every score matches the source protocol or report; each table names the instrument and score type and includes percentiles, descriptive ranges and confidence intervals with their confidence level where available; the prose interprets the pattern in plain language without contradicting the table.
Scores match the sources and are tabulated, but some tables omit percentiles, ranges or confidence intervals, or the interpretation of the pattern is thin.
Some scores are mislabeled by score type or descriptive range, scores are listed only in prose with no table, or the interpretation partly contradicts the numbers.
Scores are missing, invented, rounded or converted without basis, or do not match the sources.

rubric.criterion: Neutrality on the determination: the report presents evidence for the team without stating an eligibility decision, diagnosis or causal conclusion of its own.

levels.descriptor: No section states or implies a final eligibility decision, classification or causal conclusion; evidence for and against is presented evenly; the team's role in deciding is explicit.
No decision is stated, but some wording leans toward an outcome (for example "clearly qualifies" or "is consistent only with") or contrary evidence gets little space.
The report implies the outcome in several places, or concludes whether an exclusionary factor is the primary cause.
The report states an eligibility determination or diagnosis as fact, taking the decision away from the team.

rubric.criterion: Addresses the referral questions: the findings, eligibility summary and recommendations trace back to the stated referral concerns.

levels.descriptor: Each referral question is stated explicitly, addressed by named findings, addressed with evidence in the eligibility summary, and reflected in at least one recommendation tied to a finding.
Most referral questions are traceable through the report; one is addressed only indirectly, or a few recommendations are not tied to a finding.
The referral questions are vague or are not revisited later; recommendations are generic rather than drawn from this student's results.
No clear referral questions, and the findings and recommendations do not connect to the reason for referral.

rubric.criterion: Exclusionary factors: every required alternative explanation is addressed by name with the evidence reviewed.

levels.descriptor: Instruction (with evidence it was appropriate and delivered by qualified staff), English proficiency, sensory and motor status, cultural, environmental and economic factors, and attendance are each addressed with specific evidence (screenings, attendance data, language data, instructional history); intellectual disability and emotional disturbance are addressed when a specific learning disability is considered.
All factors are named, but one or two rely on general statements rather than cited evidence.
Several factors are missing, or are dismissed with no evidence.
Exclusionary factors are not considered, or are addressed with a single blanket statement.

rubric.criterion: Readable by the family: a parent without clinical training can follow the findings, and the student is described respectfully and in the round.

levels.descriptor: Technical terms and score scales are explained on first use; person-first, non-deficit language throughout; strengths appear alongside needs in every findings section.
Mostly accessible and respectful; a few terms go unexplained, or strengths are mentioned only in passing.
Heavy unexplained jargon or acronyms, or the student is described almost entirely in terms of deficits.
Largely inaccessible to a parent, or uses labeling or judgmental language about the student or family.
